Listen to this article Share Nigeria’s cement industry is heading for a major supply expansion, with producers expected to add 16.5 million tonnes of annual production capacity by 2028, raising the risk of intensified competition, lower capacity utilisation and slower price increases, according to a new report by CardinalStone Research. Advertisement Advertisement The investment firm projects that the combined installed capacity of cement manufacturers will increase from 65.8 million tonnes per annum (Mtpa) in 2025 to 82.3Mtpa by 2028, as leading producers accelerate investments in new plants to capture domestic and export opportunities. However, the expansion could outpace consumption in the short term, with industry capacity utilisation projected to decline from approximately 46 percent in 2026 to 43.5 percent between 2027 and 2028. The development could mark a turning point for an industry whose earnings growth has been largely supported by aggressive price increases amid elevated energy and transportation costs. In its November 25 report titled “2027 Sector Update: Capacity Growth to Reshape Supply as Pricing Momentum Fades”, CardinalStone said cement producers would increasingly depend on sales volumes, operational efficiencies, and export markets to sustain earnings as pricing momentum weakens. The report identifies Dangote Cement, BUA Cement and HBM Nigeria as key players driving the next phase of industry expansion. Advertisement Dangote Cement is targeting the commissioning of its 6 million-tonne Itori plant in Ogun State by the end of 2026, while BUA Cement plans to complete its Ososo plant in Edo State by the end of 2027. The company’s Sokoto Line 6 is expected to come on stream in 2028. For HBM Nigeria, formerly known as Lafarge Africa, new Sagamu and Ashaka production lines, adding a combined 4.5Mtpa, are expected to be commissioned in the second quarter of 2027. Advertisement According to CardinalStone, these investments are designed to take advantage of Nigeria’s growing population, relatively low cement consumption per capita and improving export opportunities. However, the additional supply could intensify the battle for market share, particularly if manufacturers prioritise higher plant utilisation over pricing discipline. Advertisement Advertisement Price increases to slow after 2026 rally The projected capacity expansion comes after cement manufacturers enjoyed significant pricing gains in 2026, helping them absorb rising energy and distribution costs. CardinalStone said realised cement prices across the three listed producers increased between 15.1 percent and 22.6 percent year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026, while combined sales volumes rose 4.4 percent to 24.6 million tonnes. The combination lifted their aggregate revenue by 22.7 percent to N4.7 trillion during the period. The research firm, however, expects price increases to moderate considerably in 2027, forecasting growth of between 8 percent and 10 percent, compared with an estimated 18.8 percent in 2026. This represents a significant slowdown from the 30.3 percent compound annual growth rate recorded in cement prices over the past five years. CardinalStone attributed the expected moderation to easing inflation, lower projected energy prices and a higher comparative base, noting that manufacturers would increasingly need to drive sales volumes rather than depend on price adjustments to grow earnings. The firm estimates Nigeria’s cement demand at approximately 33 million tonnes in 2026, up from 32 million tonnes in 2025. It expects demand growth in 2027 to receive support from government infrastructure spending, concrete road construction, lower borrowing costs following monetary easing, and improved construction activity. However, household purchasing power remains a major constraint on private construction demand, which accounts for a larger share of overall cement consumption. Infrastructure spending offers demand lifeline Public infrastructure projects are expected to provide an important source of demand for cement manufacturers as private building activity remains subdued. CardinalStone identified several ongoing highway and road construction projects, including the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway, Trans-Sahara Highway, Akwanga-Jos-Maiduguri road and Enugu-Onitsha Expressway, as potential drivers of cement consumption through 2027. The Federal Government’s growing infrastructure allocation also presents opportunities for producers, although actual budget implementation remains a significant concern. The report noted that federal capital allocation increased from N13.8 trillion in 2024 to N32.3 trillion in 2026. However, actual capital spending has lagged behind budgeted allocations, with capital budget implementation standing at 25.9 percent in the first half of 2026, compared with 84.1 percent in 2024. CardinalStone said the implementation of the 2026 capital budget had remained at zero as of the first half of the year, with government projects continuing to rely on funds released under the previous year’s capital budget. It warned that delayed releases could affect construction activity in 2027, particularly if the post-election transition slows government spending during the second and third quarters. The firm expects public spending to remain the main pillar of cement demand growth in the near term, while improved macroeconomic conditions could gradually revive private construction activity. The Central Bank of Nigeria’s Purchasing Managers’ Index also showed improving activity in the cement industry, with the subsector PMI rising from 47.7 points in August to 60.2 points in October 2026, the highest reading among the industries covered. Margins face new test as energy costs remain significant Beyond pricing and capacity expansion, manufacturers will also need to sustain operational efficiencies to protect profitability. CardinalStone said cement producers largely absorbed the energy cost shock in 2026 through higher selling prices, compressed operating costs and investments in alternative energy sources. Average EBITDA margin across the three listed producers increased by 2.3 percentage points to 55.1 percent in the first nine months of 2026. Dangote Cement’s Nigerian operations recorded an EBITDA margin of 59.8 percent, while HBM Nigeria and BUA Cement posted 44.8 percent and 52.5 percent, respectively. The report expects average sector EBITDA margin to rise to 56.4 percent in 2027, from an estimated 55 percent in 2026, supported by volume growth and cost efficiencies. Manufacturers are increasingly adopting compressed natural gas (CNG) and liquefied natural gas (LNG) to reduce their exposure to expensive diesel. About 60 percent of Dangote Cement’s domestic truck fleet now operates on CNG, with full conversion targeted for 2027. HBM Nigeria has integrated more than 500 CNG trucks into its fleet and commissioned a dedicated CNG station at Mfamosing, while BUA Cement introduced LNG-powered trucks during 2026. CinalStone estimates that fuel and power accounted for approximately 33.4 percent of the sector’s cash costs in the first nine months of 2026. Based on projected cash costs of about N5.1 trillion in 2027, the research firm estimates energy expenses at approximately N1.7 trillion, meaning every 10 percent movement in energy costs could affect sector EBITDA by about N169 billion. Export markets become strategic growth opportunity As domestic competition intensifies, exports are expected to become an increasingly important outlet for Nigeria’s cement manufacturers. Dangote Cement is positioning its new Itori facility primarily for exports, with the first phase expected to add 6 million tonnes of annual capacity. The company also plans to expand its Apapa port infrastructure to support product evacuation. The report noted that exports from Dangote Cement’s Nigerian operations increased 41.8 percent year-on-year to 1.5 million tonnes in the first nine months of 2026. Its Pan-African business also recorded a 14 percent increase in volumes to 9.1 million tonnes, supported by stronger demand in Senegal, Tanzania, Ethiopia and Congo, as well as the ramp-up of its Côte d’Ivoire facility. The company plans to expand its total production capacity from 55Mtpa to 80Mtpa by 2030, including additional investments across Nigeria and other African markets. CardinalStone said stronger export performance, particularly from Dangote Cement, could provide a buffer against domestic pricing pressure as new production lines increase supply. Chinwe Michael Chinwe Michael is a Nigerian business journalist and media professional with over 4 years of experience covering companies, financial markets, banking, fintech, economic policy, financial inclusion, and corporate affairs. She currently leads the Companies & Markets desk at BusinessDay, where she drives coverage of Nigeria’s corporate and capital markets, translates complex financial data into accessible stories, and mentors younger journalists. Prior to that, she was the head of the financial inclusion/fintech desk. With a background in banking and finance and extensive experience in media and communications, Michael has developed expertise in financial journalism, economic analysis, investigative reporting and market intelligence. Her work examines how monetary policy, corporate performance, capital flows, technology, and regulatory decisions affect businesses, investors, and households. She was selected from about 3,000 applicants as one of 20 journalists for Cohort 4 of the MTN Media Innovation Programme, gaining exposure to new approaches to journalism, technology, and media innovation. Her international journalism experience and engagement with professionals across Russia, Dubai, Saudi Arabia, and others in different sectors have further broadened her understanding of global communication and development.
